title: Dinner Without Sunlight
question: How can anything live in the dark, high-pressure deep sea?
hook: For a long time scientists assumed the deep ocean was nearly empty, and then they went to look.
idea: Deep-sea life gets by without sunlight by feeding on what sinks from above or on chemical energy at vents and seeps.

beats.prompt: A dead whale sinks to the seafloor thousands of meters down, far below the reach of light. What happens to it?

choices.label: Nothing touches it, because the deep sea is nearly lifeless
choices.feedback: That was the old assumption; research has shown significant biodiversity in the deep sea.

choices.label: It becomes a source of food and nutrients for deep-sea life
It is useless as food, since deep life needs sunlight
choices.feedback: Sunlight never reaches the deep floor; communities there run on whale falls, marine snow and chemosynthesis instead.

beats.explain: Whale falls are one of the three main sources of energy and nutrients for deep-sea communities, and the deep sea holds significant biodiversity to use them.

beats.prompt: Put these milestones in deep-sea exploration in order.
items: HMS Challenger first records the depth of the Challenger Deep
Walsh and Piccard reach the bottom in the Trieste
A chemosynthetic animal community is found at Pacific vents
The robot vehicle Kaiko reaches the bottom of the Challenger Deep
beats.explain: The depth was first recorded in 1875, the Trieste dive came in 1960, the vent community was found in 1979, and Kaiko reached the bottom in 1995.

beats.prompt: Match each ocean layer to its light conditions.
pairs: Lit, but too dim for photosynthesis
Perpetual darkness down to the seabed
beats.explain: Light fades with depth: the top layer can power photosynthesis, the twilight layer below cannot, and below that it is dark all the way to the bottom.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Below the photic zone the ocean is in perpetual darkness.
So no life can find food anywhere in the dark zone.
That is why the photic zone holds the most life.
beats.explain: Life in the dark zone can swim up to feed, live on material sinking from above, or use chemical energy at vents and seeps, so food does exist there.
